comments.why: Walter Bright on D's challenges matching C++
comments.text: Another alternative, I think is D-language bindings to QT (or betterC which is a subset of D allowes to use D with C runtime library, while retaining D-s class system, templates and memory safety). [1] [LINK] D's team is doing an incredible job of matching C++ compiler specific ABIs, name mangling/etc -- just so D users can use C++ libraries (including templates) directly from D without loosing the features of the language. comments.author: armitron
comments.story: Creating a Non-Trivial Lisp Game in 2018
comments.why: D comes closest to native C++ interop
comments.text: Rust does not have native C++ interop. C ABI is different to what clasp has done (native C++ interop). All widely used Common Lisp implementations have seamless C ABI interop through their FFIs / CFFI [1]. Clasp goes above and beyond that and natively interfaces with C++. LTO works with mixed Common Lisp and C++ code. Exception handling works as expected. You can mix Common Lisp and C++ stack frames. Correct me if I'm wrong but Rust does not have anything equivalent. The language that comes closest is D I think [2]. [1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO]

comments.author: qznc
comments.why: Shows D's C++ interop as a reason to use it
comments.text: Reasons for D: It is a way out of the C++ tar pit, because it does C++ interop better than any other language. D needs to continue to outrun C++ evolving, though. See [LINK] or [VIDEO] It has powerful meta-programming. It is effectively the opposite of Go, which does not even have generics. This certainly provides foot shooting as well, so other languages (e.g. Rust) are more conservative with that. D examples: [LINK] Those are the two reasons, which D has ahead of all other languages (ok, not Lisp wrt meta-programming). If you compare it to another specific language, there are more things to talk about.
